catalog_quote: Primary stress can be reconstructed on the second syllable of most words (McLendon 1973: 34). It falls on the initial syllable where the root is just one syllable in length; essentially, the stress does not move off the root of the word. It is likely that this pattern arose from a strictly morphological root-initial pattern; given the frequency of words containing an instrumental prefix (§5.1), this would most often correlate with the second syllable, and that generalization was extended to unprefixed roots of at least two syllables, such as *bihˈše ‘deer’ and *šiʔˈba ‘body’ (Moshinksy 1976; Buckley 2014). Continuing with these words, the pretonic syllable was deleted in Southeastern bxe, xba and Central p’še, šba; but it remains in the other languages, such as Northern biˈše, šiˈba and Eastern bi:ˈše, ši:ˈba; the last two languages largely maintain the original second-syllable stresses. Southeastern has regular initial stress, since all pretonic vowels were deleted; in Central, stress is initial in words that have lost the first vowel, but remains on the second syllable when the first vowel is preserved (as in the case of /a/): *bahˈša ‘buckeye’ > ba:ˈša compared to Southeastern bxa.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Central Pomo is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are Mithun's work on intonation and information structure, not word stress. 92 was wrong (all 21 pages are present; pp. 93-106 scanned now); it discusses intonation units, declination and the placement of salient constituents at the prosodic peak, and never states where word stress falls (stress appears only as marks on transcriptions and in one F0-trace sentence). Mithun 2020 (Benjamins SCL 94, pp. 107-126) is reachable only as a Crossref abstract, which describes prosody (pitch, intensity, rhythm) vs. grammar in Central Pomo unscripted speech; full text is paywalled/WAF-could not be reached by automated download (priority low). The best first-hand stress statement read is Buckley's 2020 draft of the De Gruyter 'Pomoan' chapter, sec. 3.6 (with Central Pomo data in his 2019 GAIL slides): stress on the second syllable of disyllabic-or-longer roots and prefixed stems, initial on unprefixed monosyllabic roots and wherever the pretonic vowel was historically deleted (p'še, šba, ʔwéni), plus initial in loans/lexical exceptions; a draft marked 'do not quote without permission', so the published 2023 chapter (DOI 10.1515/9783110712742-049, blocked here) should be checked before citation. Saved: full scanned of Mithun 1993 and the Crossref abstract record under, with updated (including the correction).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Central Pomo continues the Proto-Pomoan root-bound, left-oriented pattern: stress sits on the historically second (root) syllable, so it is peninitial when a syllabic prefix or a preserved pretonic vowel (typically /a/, lengthened) precedes (ba:ˈša, matúl, bayí:č'), and word-initial where the old first vowel has been lost or the root is an unprefixed monosyllable (p'še, šba, mšémšew, lówa:č'a:č'); loans and some lexical items are initial-stressed. Buckley's slides analyse this as left-edge extrametricality with stress at the left edge, blocked by a monosyllabic unprefixed root, plus lexical exceptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Central Pomo (alternating secondary stress is mentioned only for Eastern Pomo in the slides).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords stressed initially (sómle:lo < Sp. sombrero, háyu 'dog'); 'lexical exceptions – extrametricality blocked for certain roots'; forms like ʔúda:w 'lots' initial 'for other reasons' (Buckley 2019 slides 30-31). Vowel length has no effect on placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress computed from the left edge of the word/root; suffixation does not shift it (root-bound). Statement is from a comparative family chapter drawing on McLendon 1973, Moshinsky 1976, Oswalt 1964 and Mithun's stress-marked Central Pomo data, not from a dedicated Central Pomo grammar (Mithun's grammar remains in preparation).
new_statements.identity_note: Statement concerns Central Pomo as a whole (cent2138) within a family survey; Buckley's Central Pomo forms come from Mithun's published material (speakers from Hopland and Yokaya rancherias) and he notes pretonic /a/ length is 'mainly in the coastal dialect (Marianne Mithun, p.c.)'. No dialect-specific stress differences are claimed. The file quoted is the author's December 2020 draft of the chapter published in 2023 (De Gruyter, ch. 49, pp. 1223-1246); the draft header asks not to be quoted without permission, so wording/page should be verified against the published chapter before any external quotation.

new_statements.reading: Central Pomo keeps the Proto-Pomo pattern: primary stress on the second syllable of disyllabic-or-longer roots and of prefix+root stems (matúl 'old lady', maʔá 'food', ba-yí:č' 'learned to talk'), on the first syllable of unprefixed monosyllabic roots (lówa:č'a:č', mítaq'), and on the first syllable wherever the historical pretonic vowel was deleted (p'še 'deer', šba 'body', ʔwéni 'yesterday' < *duwéni) plus loans and some lexical exceptions (sómle:lo 'hat', háju 'dog'). Buckley's 2019 analysis: left-edge extrametricality with stress at the left edge of the remaining domain, blocked by an unprefixed monosyllabic root; vowel length has no effect. So the language is a fixed: second syllable-syllable system with a morphologically/historically conditioned initial alternative, i.e. 'second syllable unless the first syllable is (or was) the root', which surfaces as frequent initial stress. Caveat: the source is an author draft marked 'do not quote without permission'; wording should be checked against the published 2023 chapter before external citation. Neither of the two works with stress in the title (Mithun 1993, Mithun 2020) states a stress rule; this statement comes from material already held by the project from our earlier reading, re-verified against the PDF text.

new_statements.quote: Pn, Pc, Pne, and Pe have a phonemic accent that occurs mostly on the first or second syllable of a word. It is primarily a pitch accent (tone) in Pn and stress in Pc, Pne, and Pe. In Pe its location is partially predictable morphologically: stress always occurs on the root in verbs. There is, however, no synchronic basis for identifying roots in most nouns. Halpern (MS) suggests that the same pattern of partial morphological predictability also exists in Pn, Pc and Pne. [p. 34-35:] The predictable location of stress in Pse appears to have arisen through the operation of a simple phonological rule (cf. 141.1) that seems also to have applied in Pc, but not as completely: pre-tonic vowels are deleted. [...] Thus many proto forms which were accented on the second syllable became Pn, Pc, Pe, and Pne initially accented syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Buckley-based reading (second syllable of prefix+root stems, initial for unprefixed monosyllabic roots and where the historical pretonic vowel was deleted; 'the stress does not move off the root'). McLendon adds: (a) the accent is phonemic and only partially predictable (root-based, per Halpern); (b) it is realised as stress in Pc, unlike the pitch accent of Pn; (c) the mechanism -- pretonic vowel deletion in Pc, 'not as completely' as in Pse -- by which second-syllable-accented proto forms became initially accented, which is exactly Buckley's 'initial where the first vowel was lost' clause. Buckley's 'second syllable of most words' reconstruction, cited to McL…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Central Pomo (Pc) has a phonemic (contrastive) stress accent, realised as stress rather than pitch, that falls mostly on the first or second syllable of the word; following Halpern (MS), its position is only partially predictable, on the morphological principle that stress sits on the root (fully stated for Eastern Pomo verbs). Diachronically, Central Pomo deleted pretonic vowels (less completely than Southeastern Pomo), so Proto-Pomo forms accented on the second syllable often surface with initial accent, while Pc, with Pn, Pe and Pne, 'preserved the phonemic status of the proto prosodic feature'. The Central Pomo phoneme inventory table lists 'stress /'/' as a phoneme.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in Central Pomo; a 'secondary accent' is mentioned only for two reconstructed Proto-Pomo compounds (ASHES, TEARS).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is called phonemic and only 'partially' morphologically predictable (no synchronic basis for identifying roots in most nouns, said of Pe and extended to Pc via Halpern). Forms 'borrowed with initial stress, as Oswalt mentions in his article (1964a)' are noted in the same section (the sentence's subject is Pk, Kashaya; Oswalt 1964a compares Kashaya with Central Pomo, so the remark may cover Pc too, but the fragment does not say so).
new_statements.identity_note: McLendon's 'Pc' is Central Pomo as recorded by Robert Oswalt and A. M. Halpern (the book's informant table); no sub-dialect is named. The stress sentences are comparative statements covering Pn, Pc, Pne and Pe together; the fully explicit root rule is stated for Eastern Pomo (Pe) verbs and extended to Pc only on Halpern's (MS) authority.

sources.quote: Prosody (pitch, intensity, rhythm) involves continua and can be more responsive to certain subtle differences in cognitive state, discourse context, and interactive goals. Grammar (morphology and syntax) can mark more distinctions, but these are categorical and conventionalized ... Here some prosodic structures, their functions, and their relation to grammatical structures are discussed with examples from Central Pomo, a language indigenous to Northern California.
sources.note: Abstract only: the chapter is about prosodic structure (intonation units, pitch/intensity/rhythm) versus grammatical structure in unscripted Central Pomo speech, i.e. the same theme as Mithun 1993.
